yearsToFirstCrop.notes: No transferable planting-to-first-food age. Trial days after sowing are accession, place and season specific, not a perennial age curve.

yearsToFullBearing.notes: No universal full-bearing age applies to this annual or dual-purpose crop.

yieldKgPerTreeMature.notes: Trial grain kg/ha is retained as a reference only; it is not kg/plant or household food yield.

chillUnits.notes: No numeric crop-specific chilling requirement is verified.

pollination.notes: No household-food pollination classification is inferred from a grain trial.

harvestProduct: seed/grain; household food requires confirmed food-qualified sweet material and preparation

supplementaryReferences.title: SA sweet narrow-leaf field grain and harvest
supplementaryReferences.quote: At Riversdale the lupins were harvested directly on 29 October
supplementaryReferences.doc: Hardy et al.: Lupino 19 (September 2004), Crop Management, Harvesting, Tables 1–2
supplementaryReferences.note: Southern Cape 2003 rotation trial, sweet narrow-leaf Tanjil. Actual sowing / harvested grain kg/ha across camps: Riversdale 15 April / 2401–2529; Swellendam 12 May / 1003–1289; Tygerhoek 24 April / 2584–3058. Swellendam bracketed 1407–1704 figures estimate harvest losses, not weighed harvest. Riversdale’s 29 October harvest is an observed date, not generic maturity or a current-cultivar picking window. Feed-laboratory grain analysis does not certify household edible production.

supplementaryReferences.title: Current supplier cultivar discussion
supplementaryReferences.doc: Agricol: Sweet Lupins — narrow leaf, Information section
supplementaryReferences.note: Supplier lists Mandellup and Lila-Baer, April–May planting, feed and green-manure uses. Its whole-SA region claim is not an independently verified climate-by-climate food trial. Tanjil’s earlier field amounts and dates are not transferred to these cultivars.

supplementaryReferences.title: Narrow-leaf sweet and bitter types differ
supplementaryReferences.doc: DAFF: Legume poster, lupin column, Description and Uses rows
supplementaryReferences.note: The narrow-leaf species includes sweet low-alkaloid and bitter high-alkaloid types. Its botanical identity alone does not qualify the seed as household food. White-lupin advice belongs to a different species; old availability statements are not treated as current facts.

supplementaryReferences.title: Food qualification and preparation
supplementaryReferences.doc: BfR: Alkaloids and allergies — current data on health risks from lupin seeds in food, 17 September 2025, section 3.2.1.1.4
supplementaryReferences.note: The primary food-risk assessment cannot supply a generally validated household debittering method. Use food-qualified seed/product and appropriate preparation confirmed with a qualified adviser; this is a product-care reference, not South African legislation or a home-processing recipe.

productionGuidance.products: seed/grain; household food requires confirmed food-qualified sweet material and preparation
care: Confirm sweet versus bitter material and food versus feed purpose before including this planting in household food.
Keep narrow-leaf recommendations separate from white lupin. Generic grain and green-manure research does not supply edible kg or a plant age curve.
purchase: Ask the supplier about identified sweet narrow-leaf material and whether it is qualified for the intended food use. Current Mandellup/Lila-Baer options are supplier context, not calibrated local food-yield predictions.
